methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

New searches prioritize areas underrepresented relative to the last five completed STOC and FOCS editions. Conference shares guide collection; paper counts and open-problem counts are different quantities.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large groups of 50 and 25 named small groups of 20: all 1,000 planned places are assigned to named categories. These are future targets. Preliminary editorial pruning is recorded in the large- and small-category manifests under to_delete/; final quota selection and a complete deduplication audit have not been performed. Topic assignments use original subjects, saved questions and primary source titles. Unclear cases go to Miscellaneous. General combinatorics outside the accepted scope is archived with a reason. Preliminary removals retain their reason and pre-removal selection category separately from original subject labels. Archived records remain accessible through the Selection scope filter and full exports. Original categories and stable IDs are preserved. Classification does not verify the statement or its current open status.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

cards.title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
cards.answer_criterion: Answer yes by proving one finite constant valid for all dimensions, measures, and test functions. Answer no by constructing isotropic log-concave measures and test functions whose variance-to-gradient-energy ratios are unbounded. Proving the inequality only for linear or quadratic functions, or with a factor growing with n, does not resolve this statement.
cards.context:
The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.
cards.why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.
Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques.
Klartag proves ψμ=O(√log n), equivalently C_P(μ)=O(log n), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality.
Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).

cards.title: How many k-element subsets can a line separate from a planar point set?
cards.formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove an upper bound for every admissible planar point set and a lower-bound construction for each admissible n,k that match within absolute constant factors. Resolving only fixed k, only the balanced case k=⌊n/2⌋, or only the exponent while leaving an unbounded factor between the bounds is partial progress.
cards.context:
A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

importance.reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.

progress.text: Dey proves K₂(n,k)=O(n k^(1/3)) for 1≤k≤n/2 through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an O(n^(4/3)) upper bound.
Tóth constructs planar point sets with n exp(Ω(√log k)) k-sets for n≥2k>0, improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows.
Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce n^(1+ε) halving edges for any fixed positive ε.

Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains 4/3.
The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.

cards.title: Hill’s conjecture for the crossing number of complete graphs
cards.formal: For every integer n≥3, is the minimum number of edge crossings in a drawing of the complete graph K_n in the plane exactly $H(n)=\frac14\prod_{i=0}^{3}\left\lfloor\frac{n-i}{2}\right\rfloor$? Edges may be arbitrary simple curves. Drawings with H(n) crossings are known for every n; the unresolved assertion is that no drawing has fewer.
cards.definitions: K_n has n vertices and one edge between each pair of distinct vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points of ℝ² to its vertices and represents each edge by a simple arc joining its endpoints, with no other vertex on the arc. Edge interiors intersect in finitely many points, all proper crossings; tangencies, shared subarcs and crossings of three or more edge interiors are excluded. Count intersection points of edge interiors, not shared graph endpoints. The crossing number cr(K_n) is the minimum over all these drawings and all vertex placements. Finite polygonal arcs suffice; restricting every edge to a single straight segment is a different problem. Allowing drawings on the sphere with arbitrary arcs gives the same minimum. H(n)=n⁴/64+O(n³), but the card asks for exact equality at every n, not just agreement of leading coefficients. For example H(5)=1, H(6)=3, H(12)=150 and H(13)=225.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove cr(K_n)≥H(n) for every n, or exhibit one valid drawing of some K_n with strictly fewer than H(n) crossings. An asymptotic ratio of 1 would settle only the asymptotic version; a lower bound for straight-line, two-page, or shortest-geodesic drawings does not by itself settle arbitrary drawings.
cards.context:
A complete graph asks every pair of vertices to communicate through a separate drawn edge. Planarity fails already at five vertices. The conjecture proposes an exact measure of the unavoidable interference as the number of vertices grows, independent of the choice of drawing coordinates or the shape of each edge.

The upper bound is constructive: there are systematic drawings with H(n) crossings. The challenge is universal. A lower bound must rule out every different way to route the edges, including configurations whose geometry bears little resemblance to the known constructions. Counting crossings in a visually natural drawing establishes only the upper bound.

The topological and geometric versions must be separated. Straight-line edges impose extra restrictions; shortest arcs on a sphere allow more freedom but still impose a geometric rule. Two-page drawings impose another rule: vertices lie on one spine and each edge stays on one of its two sides. Proving the formula for any of these families narrows the search for a counterexample without exhausting arbitrary curves.

General lower bounds are already close to the conjectured leading term. The flag-algebra approach derives inequalities from the frequencies and compatibility of small drawing configurations. Even a remaining gap of roughly one or two percent matters here: the goal is an exact extremal formula for all sizes, rather than a constant-factor estimate.

The April 2025 spherical-arc theorem is a substantial geometric advance: it establishes the conjectured lower bound for every shortest-geodesic drawing on the sphere. Its statement does not say that an optimal unrestricted drawing must be of this type. That missing reduction is why the original question remains open.
cards.why: This is a basic benchmark for universal crossing lower bounds. Its study links topological graph drawing, geometric configurations, and extremal counting methods, and supplies a reference family against which crossing inequalities for more general graphs are compared.

importance.reason: A foundational exact extremal problem for the most symmetric dense graph family. It tests the reach of general crossing-number lower bounds beyond drawing classes constrained by a particular geometry.

progress.text: Hill’s constructions and subsequent work give drawings with H(n) crossings. The general assertion that these are optimal became the Hill or Harary–Hill conjecture, also known as Guy’s conjecture.
Ábrego, Aichholzer, Fernández-Merchant, Ramos, and Salazar prove that the two-page crossing number of K_n equals H(n). The unrestricted crossing number minimizes over a larger drawing class.

Balogh, Lidický, and Salazar use flag algebras to show an asymptotic general lower bound of at least 0.985H(n). This substantially improves the earlier general asymptotic ratio, while leaving a positive gap from the conjectured value.
The Gasarch–Hayes–Ostuni–Park column states the unrestricted formula as Conjecture 4.6. The linked manuscript is dated 4 January 2025, correcting the legacy record’s 2022 source year.

Streltsova and Wagner prove the lower bound H(n) for all spherical shortest-geodesic drawings, with equality for coneighborly configurations. Their introduction still lists the unrestricted conjecture as open and verified through n=12.

references.title: Sublevels in arrangements and the spherical arc crossing number of complete graphs
references.authors: Elizaveta Streltsova; Uli Wagner

cards.status_note: The April 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves arbitrary drawings unresolved while proving the spherical-arc case. No general proof or counterexample located through 10 September 2026. Restricted drawing-class results are not treated as full resolutions.

context_blocks.text: A complete graph asks every pair of vertices to communicate through a separate drawn edge. Planarity fails already at five vertices. The conjecture proposes an exact measure of the unavoidable interference as the number of vertices grows, independent of the choice of drawing coordinates or the shape of each edge.

The upper bound is constructive: there are systematic drawings with H(n) crossings. The challenge is universal. A lower bound must rule out every different way to route the edges, including configurations whose geometry bears little resemblance to the known constructions. Counting crossings in a visually natural drawing establishes only the upper bound.

The topological and geometric versions must be separated. Straight-line edges impose extra restrictions; shortest arcs on a sphere allow more freedom but still impose a geometric rule. Two-page drawings impose another rule: vertices lie on one spine and each edge stays on one of its two sides. Proving the formula for any of these families narrows the search for a counterexample without exhausting arbitrary curves.

General lower bounds are already close to the conjectured leading term. The flag-algebra approach derives inequalities from the frequencies and compatibility of small drawing configurations. Even a remaining gap of roughly one or two percent matters here: the goal is an exact extremal formula for all sizes, rather than a constant-factor estimate.

The April 2025 spherical-arc theorem is a substantial geometric advance: it establishes the conjectured lower bound for every shortest-geodesic drawing on the sphere. Its statement does not say that an optimal unrestricted drawing must be of this type. That missing reduction is why the original question remains open.

cards.title: Can circle–segment reporting on connected planar graphs have additive output cost?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic static data structure that preprocesses a connected straight-line planar graph with n >= 2 edges in $O(n\log^3 n)$ time and space and reports all k edges intersecting a query circle in $O(\log^3 n+k)$ worst-case time? The graph is embedded in the Euclidean plane: edges are nonzero closed line segments, distinct edge interiors are disjoint, and edges meet only at shared endpoints. A query supplies a center c and radius r > 0. Promise that the circle contains no graph vertex on its boundary and is tangent to no edge. Report each intersected input edge once. All hidden constants are independent of the graph, circle, and output size.
cards.definitions: The query circle is the boundary $\{p:\|p-c\|_2=r\}$, not the filled disk. An edge intersects it if at least one point of that segment lies on the boundary, including when both edge endpoints are outside the disk. k counts distinct reported edges, even if one segment has two intersection points. Connectivity is that of the graph with the specified endpoints as vertices; crossing edges without a shared vertex are excluded. Use a unit-cost real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square roots, and comparisons, together with random access and O(log n)-bit integer indices. Each stored real or integer occupies one cell; integer bit manipulation does not apply to arbitrary real values. Preprocessing includes construction of every auxiliary index. Queries return edge identifiers and use only the stored structure and the query. The target specializes the older connected-segment direction to planar input and removes a multiplicative output overhead from a later bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure with all three stated worst-case bounds, or prove that no such data structure exists in this model. An O((k+1) log^3 n) query bound still incurs the overhead this proposition asks to remove. Improvements only for disks, approximate answers, or a restricted family of graph embeddings do not establish the positive answer.
cards.context:
A large circle can enclose many graph edges while crossing very few of them. Reporting every segment inside its disk can therefore be far more expensive than the requested boundary query. There is also a second geometric obstacle: a segment can cross the circle twice while both of its endpoints are outside. An index of endpoint locations alone does not identify every answer.

Connectivity gives the search more structure. If a connected piece of the graph contains vertices on both sides of the circle, then some edge crosses the boundary. This observation suggests organizing the input into connected pieces and using geometric tests to discard pieces containing no answer. Planarity is an additional promise in this card; the graph is not an arbitrary collection of crossing segments.

The ISAAC 2025 construction makes this strategy effective using a hierarchy of connected edge subsets. Its preprocessing depends on n plus the number of edge crossings, and its reporting bound is O((k+1) log^3 n), including the empty-output case. With planar input the crossing term disappears. The remaining target here is to pay the logarithmic search overhead once per query, then only constant additional cost per reported edge.

This is a sharper question than the broad direction recorded at the May 2025 seminar. The later paper already demonstrates that connectivity can improve the old bounds substantially. Its final section discusses faster repeated searches and lower bounds. The precise additive-output target, fixed preprocessing budget, and nondegenerate-query promise here are editorial choices that turn that remaining direction into a yes/no proposition.
cards.why: Output-sensitive reporting separates the unavoidable cost of listing answers from the cost of finding them. This question asks whether connected planar structure is strong enough to achieve that separation for a curved boundary query, combining topological promises with geometric searching.

importance.reason: A focused structural reporting problem: removing per-answer search overhead would clarify the algorithmic value of connected planar input. It is narrower than general range-searching trade-off questions.

progress.text: Storandt proposes exploiting connectivity for circle–segment queries. The stored draft originally described this broad direction without a fixed remaining target.

Afshani, Bosch, and Storandt obtain O((n+C) log^3 n) preprocessing time and space for C crossings, and O((k+1) log^3 n) reporting. Thus the historical direction has substantial positive progress; Theorem 8 is not the additive-output bound asked here.
